The Romans aren't killing other people; they're killing each other. Wars help maintain equilibrium by reducing elite overproduction. First, wars create social cohesion and a hatred of the other, giving life meaning. They also provide social mobility—poor individuals can become wealthy through war. Wars lead to wealth destruction, creating opportunities for survival of the fittest. High fertility rates result from many deaths, as mothers are forced to have more children. Wars release social tension; enemies become best friends after fighting together. Nobility enjoys wars like a chess game, with the worst outcome being becoming hostages.

After Carthage's destruction, Romans turned against each other in civil wars, starting with the Social Wars where Roman allies rebelled because they were not granted citizenship. The Roman state had to give in and grant citizenship, marking one of Rome’s most radical turning points. Massive inequality existed; nobility controlled land and slaves while peasants struggled. Tiberius Gracchus proposed redistributing public land to the poor, but was beaten to death by the nobility who claimed the land as their own.

Dictators like Marius promised reforms but failed to deliver. Sulla killed reformers to solve social conflicts. Caesar, born wealthy and ambitious, used discontent to build his political career through bribery, aiming for a generalship to invade Gaul.
